scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

prediction.raw: In reflecting on the situation, it's clear that while you have the right to choose your wedding attire, the way you expressed your reasons to your mom was hurtful and may have strained your relationship. Here's a structured approach to address the situation: 1. **Acknowledge Your Right to Choose**: It's important that you feel comfortable and confident on your wedding day. Your choice of attire should reflect your personality and preferences. 2. **Consider Emotional Impact**: Your mom likely felt hurt when you associated her divorce with her choice of wedding dress. It's important to recognize that her feelings were valid and that her choices do not define your own. 3. **Reframe the Conversation**: Instead of blaming her for your choice, focus on explaining your personal preference for colored dresses. Emphasize that it's about your comfort and style, not about her past choices. 4. **Seek a Compromise**: Consider discussing your preferences with your mom in a way that respects both your feelings and hers. Perhaps find a compromise that allows you to wear a colored dress while acknowledging her desire to participate in the wedding planning. 5. **Communicate Constructively**: Revisit the conversation when emotions have calmed. Apologize for how your words made her feel and explain your perspective in a more constructive manner. This can help mend the relationship and ensure both parties feel heard and respected. In conclusion, while it's your right to choose your wedding attire, the manner in which you expressed your reasons was hurtful. Approaching the situation with empathy and constructive communication can help resolve the issue and strengthen your relationship with your mom.

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me to tell my mom that she's the reason I won't wear a white dress to my wedding. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, I'm engaged and planning a small, semi-formal beach wedding. My mom suggested going to a bridal shop in town to pick out a wedding dress, and she was really excited about it. But I told her I don't want a white dress because the shop only sells white dresses. I already looked into it, so I know that's their specialty. I think the whole idea of white wedding dresses is kind of silly. It started with Queen Victoria, so it's not some ancient tradition. Plus, the symbolism of white meaning purity, innocence, or virginity is outdated and doesn't resonate with me. I mean, why should the color of my dress define my worth or my marital status? But the main reason I'm against a white dress is personal. My mom wore a white dress when she got married, and now she's divorced. Every other woman in my family has worn a colored dressâĢĶusually blue or red, either really pale or really dark. And they've all had long, mostly happy marriages, some even until death. So, seeing that pattern, I feel like a white dress might not be the best choice for me. When my mom asked why I didn't want a white dress, I first mentioned the Queen Victoria thing, but she didn't think that was enough. Then I said I'm not exactly "innocent," which was a really awkward conversation to have with my mom. She said that wasn't good enough either, so I finally told her that I just don't like white dresses, think colored dresses look nicer, and it's my wedding, so I should get to pick my clothes. But she kept asking, and eventually, I admitted that her being the only one to break the tradition and also the only one to get divorced didn't exactly make me confident in white dresses. She got really quiet, and I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologized yet, but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the first three perfectly fine answers I gave. I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with because it's my wedding, and the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiancÃ©. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first three answers, I wouldn't be in this situation. So, is it AITA (Ask If Tolerable, Assume Not) to tell my mom that she's the reason I won't wear a white dress? Hmm, I need to think about this. On one hand, I have the right to choose what I wear on my wedding day. It's my big day, and I should feel comfortable and confident in my choices. On the other hand, my mom is likely feeling hurt and upset because I associated her divorce with her choice of wedding dress, which might make her feel like her choices negatively impacted me. I also need to consider the emotional impact of my words. Telling my mom that her being the only one to break the tradition and get divorced made me not want a white dress could be really hurtful. It might make her feel like her actions are reflected in my choices, which could strain our relationship. Maybe I should approach this differently. Instead of blaming her for my choice, I could explain that I prefer colored dresses for personal reasons and that it's important for me to feel comfortable on my wedding day. I could acknowledge her feelings and perhaps find a compromise or a way to respect both our preferences. In the end, communication is key. It's important to express my feelings without making my mom feel attacked or responsible for my choices. Maybe I can revisit the conversation when things have calmed down and apologize for how I made her feel, while also explaining my perspective in a more constructive way.
